lesson.title: The Tank Circuit: Why Parallel LC Peaks Instead of Dips
lesson.summary: In a parallel RLC circuit, resonance produces the opposite effect of a series RLC circuit: instead of minimum impedance, the circuit reaches its maximum impedance, because the inductor and capacitor currents largely cancel each other while energy circulates between the two elements.
lesson.body:
You already know from Resonance and RLC Circuit that a series RLC circuit reaches a special frequency where the inductor's reactance and the capacitor's reactance cancel exactly, leaving only resistance. Parallel resonance asks the same question from the other side: what happens when the inductor and capacitor are connected in parallel instead of in series, the arrangement you studied in Parallel Circuits.

In a parallel circuit it is easier to work with admittance, the reciprocal of impedance, than with impedance directly, because the admittances of parallel branches simply add. The admittance of a parallel RLC circuit is Y = 1/R + jωC + 1/(jωL), which can be rewritten as Y = 1/R + j(ωC minus 1/(ωL)). The imaginary part is the net susceptance, and it vanishes at the same condition as series resonance, ωC = 1/(ωL), so ω0 = 1/√(LC), or in ordinary frequency, f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). The resonant frequency formula is identical to the series case. What changes is what happens to impedance at that frequency.

With the susceptance gone, all that remains is the conductance 1/R, so the total impedance at resonance is purely resistive and equal to R itself, which is the maximum impedance the circuit can present. Physically, at f0 the inductor and capacitor exchange energy back and forth between magnetic and electric fields every cycle, and the current flowing into the L branch is nearly equal and opposite to the current flowing into the C branch at every instant. Those two large branch currents mostly cancel where the branches join, so only a small current, just enough to replace the energy lost in R, needs to flow from the source. Because the source sees very little current for a given applied voltage, it sees a high impedance. This is why a parallel resonant circuit is often called a tank circuit: energy sloshes back and forth inside the LC tank while the external source barely notices.

Consider a parallel RLC circuit with L = 50 mH, C = 220 nF, and a 2 kΩ resistor. The resonant frequency is f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). The product LC = 0.05 times 220 times 10 to the minus 9, which is 1.1 times 10 to the minus 8. Its square root is 1.049 times 10 to the minus 4, so f0 = 1/(2π times 1.049 times 10 to the minus 4), about 1517 Hz, roughly 1.52 kHz. The sharpness of that impedance peak is set by the quality factor Q = R/(ω0L) = 2000/(2π times 1517 times 0.05) = 2000/476.7, approximately 4.2, which you can also get from Q = Rω0C, giving the same value. A Q of about 4 means the impedance peak is noticeable but not razor sharp, pushing R higher or choosing an L and C with a larger L to C ratio would sharpen it further.

This maximum-impedance, energy-sloshing behavior of a parallel resonant tank is exactly the mechanism used inside notch filters, which block a single unwanted frequency, and some band-pass and band-reject filters, all covered in the chapters ahead.
